questions.q: Arrange in order of decreasing reactivity towards aqueous NaOH: (I) chlorobenzene, (II) 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene, (III) 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene, (IV) 1-chloro-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene.
questions.explain: Each nitro group ortho or para to Cl spreads the negative charge of the Meisenheimer complex onto its oxygens, so more such groups mean faster SNAr. Plain chlorobenzene needs about 623 K and 300 atm.

questions.q: Which substituent on chlorobenzene does NOT appreciably speed up its reaction with OH⁻ by the SNAr route?
questions.explain: The carbanion charge is delocalised only onto the carbons ortho and para to the site of attack, so a meta nitro group cannot take it up and has little effect on the rate.

questions.q: Which statement about the SNAr reaction of 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene with hydroxide is correct?
options: Cl⁻ leaves first to give an aryl cation
The nucleophile attacks from the back of the C–Cl bond in one step
Addition of OH⁻ to the ipso carbon is the slow step and makes that carbon sp³
questions.explain: SNAr is addition–elimination: OH⁻ adds to the carbon bearing Cl (slow), giving the Meisenheimer complex, and Cl⁻ then leaves quickly. The ring blocks backside attack, and an aryl cation is very unstable.

questions.q: 4-Chlorotoluene is heated with NaOH at about 340 °C. An equal mixture of 3-methylphenol and 4-methylphenol is obtained. This shows that the reaction goes by:
options: An ArSN1 route through an aryl cation
Neighbouring group participation of the methyl group
questions.explain: Addition–elimination would put OH only where Cl was, giving 4-methylphenol alone. The 3-isomer appears because a benzyne forms and OH⁻ adds to either end of the triple bond; true SNAr needs activating groups.
